passages.quote: A heat exchanger is a component that allows the transfer of heat from one fluid (liquid or gas) to another fluid.
Heat can flow only from the hotter to the cooler fluid.
In a heat exchanger there is no direct contact between the two fluids.
Although heat exchangers come in every shape and size imaginable, the construction of most heat exchangers fall into one of two categories: tube and shell, or plate.
This type of heat exchanger consists of a set of tubes in a container called a shell.
At the ends of the tubes, the tube side fluid is separated from the shell side fluid by the tube sheet(s).
In systems where the two fluids are at vastly different pressures, the higher pressure fluid is typically directed through the tubes and the lower pressure fluid is circulated on the shell side.
The support plates shown on Figure 1 also act as baffles to direct the flow of fluid within the shell back and forth across the tubes.
A plate type heat exchanger, as illustrated in Figure 2, consists of plates instead of tubes to separate the hot and cold fluids.
Note that the hottest cold-fluid temperature is always less than the coldest hot-fluid temperature.
Counter flow heat exchangers are the most efficient of the three types.

Cross flow, as illustrated in Figure 5, exists when one fluid flows perpendicular to the second fluid; that is, one fluid flows through tubes and the second fluid passes around the tubes at 90° angle.
Cross flow heat exchangers are usually found in applications where one of the fluids changes state (2-phase flow).
In actuality, most large heat exchangers are not purely parallel flow, counter flow, or cross flow; they are usually a combination of the two or all three types of heat exchangers.
When a heat exchanger's fluids pass each other more than once, a heat exchanger is called a multi-pass heat exchanger.
If the fluids pass each other only once, the heat exchanger is called a single-pass heat exchanger.
A regenerative heat exchanger is one in which the same fluid is both the cooling fluid and the cooled fluid, as illustrated in Figure 7.
In a nonregenerative heat exchanger, as illustrated in Figure 7, the hot fluid is cooled by fluid from a separate system and the energy (heat) removed is not returned to the system.

It is important to remember that the term regenerative/nonregenerative only refers to "how" a heat exchanger functions in a system, and does not indicate any single type (tube and shell, plate, parallel flow, counter flow, etc.).

Some of the more common applications are found in heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems, radiators on internal combustion engines, boilers, condensers, and as preheaters or coolers in fluid systems.
The fins improve the efficiency of a heat exchanger
All air conditioning systems contain at least two heat exchangers, usually called the evaporator and the condenser.

Preheating in stages increases the plant's efficiency and minimizes thermal shock stress to components, as compared to injecting ambient temperature liquid into a boiler or other device that operates at high temperatures.
It is a closed space into which the steam exits the turbine and is forced to give up its latent heat of vaporization.
The difference between the saturation temperature for the existing condenser vacuum and the temperature of the condensate is termed condensate depression.
The bottom area of the condenser is the hotwell, as shown in Figure 9.
Condensers operate at a vacuum to ensure the temperature (and thus the pressure) of the steam is as low as possible.
This maximizes the ∆T and ∆P between the source and the heat sink, ensuring the highest cycle efficiency possible.
If noncondensable gasses are allowed to build up in the condenser, vacuum will decrease and the saturation temperature at which the steam will condense increases.
Admit the colder fluid to the heat exchanger first, followed by the hotter fluid.

body.text: To transfer heat, the fluids must be at different temperatures and must come into thermal contact.
The heat moves from the hot fluid to the metal isolating the two fluids, and then to the cooler fluid.

checks.q: How does heat get from one fluid to the other in a heat exchanger?
o: Through a third fluid in the shell
From the hot fluid to the metal between them, then to the cooler fluid
By direct mixing of the two fluids
From the cooler fluid to the hotter fluid
checks.x: There is no direct contact between the two fluids. The heat is transferred from the hot fluid to the metal isolating the two fluids and then to the cooler fluid.

body.text: The tube and shell is the most basic and most common type.

body.alt: Tube and shell heat exchanger cut open, labeling the tube sheet, support plates, steam inlet, feedwater connections, and water box.

body.text: The fluid inside the tubes is the tube side fluid, and the fluid outside them is the shell side fluid.
Tubes are rolled and press-fitted or welded into the tube sheet to give a leak tight seal.
This is due to economy, because tubes can be made to withstand higher pressures than the shell for a much lower cost.

body.alt: Plate heat exchanger: a stack of plates with gaskets between frame ends, with hot and cold fluids alternating between plates.

body.text: Hot and cold fluids alternate between the plates, and baffles direct the flow. The large plate area lets a plate unit transfer much more heat than a similarly sized tube and shell unit.

checks.q: What are the two types of heat exchanger construction?
o: Regenerative and non-regenerative
Tube and shell, and plate
Parallel and counter flow
Single-pass and multi-pass
checks.x: The construction of most heat exchangers falls into one of two categories: tube and shell, or plate.

checks.q: What separates the tube side fluid from the shell side fluid at the ends of the tubes?
o: The shell
The support plates
The tube sheet
The baffles
checks.x: At the ends of the tubes, the tube side fluid is separated from the shell side fluid by the tube sheet(s).

checks.q: What do baffles do in a tube and shell heat exchanger?
o: Seal the tubes to the tube sheet
Separate the tube side fluid from the shell
Hold the higher pressure fluid
Direct the fluid back and forth across the tubes
checks.x: The support plates also act as baffles to direct the flow of fluid within the shell back and forth across the tubes.

body.text: Parallel flow exists when both fluids flow in the same direction. They enter from the same end with a large temperature difference, and their temperatures approach each other.

body.alt: Parallel flow: both fluids enter at the same end, and a graph shows their temperatures closing toward each other along the length.

body.text: Counter flow exists when the two fluids flow in opposite directions, entering at opposite ends. The cooler fluid leaves where the hot fluid enters, so it approaches the hot fluid's inlet temperature.

body.alt: Counter flow: the fluids enter at opposite ends, and a graph shows a nearly constant temperature difference along the length.

body.text: A counter flow unit can have the hottest cold-fluid temperature greater than the coldest hot-fluid temperature.

body.alt: Cross flow: one fluid passes through tubes while the other crosses them at a right angle, with a graph of both temperatures.

body.text: Counter flow is the most efficient per unit surface area because the average temperature difference between the fluids over the length of the exchanger is maximized.

checks.q: In a parallel flow heat exchanger, how do the two fluids flow?
o: At 90° to each other
Back and forth through U bends only
In the same direction
In opposite directions
checks.x: Parallel flow exists when both the tube side fluid and the shell side fluid flow in the same direction.

checks.q: In which arrangement can the hottest cold-fluid temperature exceed the coldest hot-fluid temperature?
o: Only in a regenerative unit
Counter flow
Parallel flow
Neither arrangement
checks.x: In contrast to parallel flow, a counter flow heat exchanger can have the hottest cold-fluid temperature greater than the coldest hot-fluid temperature.

checks.q: Where are cross flow heat exchangers usually found?
o: Only in small oil coolers
Only in plate construction
Where one of the fluids changes state
Where both fluids stay liquid at low flow
checks.x: Cross flow heat exchangers are usually found in applications where one of the fluids changes state.

body.alt: Single-pass unit with straight tubes, and multi-pass unit with fluid reversing through U bends and shell baffles.

body.text: A multi-pass unit commonly reverses the flow in the tubes with U bends. Baffles on the shell side give the same effect for the shell side fluid.

The hot fluid leaving a system gives up its heat to reheat the fluid returning to the system. These units are usually found in high temperature systems where part of the fluid is removed from the main process and then returned.

body.alt: Two process diagrams: in the regenerative unit the outgoing fluid heats the returning fluid, and in the non-regenerative unit a separate cooling system removes the heat.

checks.q: What makes a heat exchanger multi-pass?
o: Its fluids pass each other more than once
It has more than one shell
It uses two different fluids
It has plates instead of tubes
checks.x: When a heat exchanger's fluids pass each other more than once, it is called a multi-pass heat exchanger.

checks.q: What defines a regenerative heat exchanger?
o: The same fluid is both the cooling fluid and the cooled fluid
The hot fluid is cooled by a separate system
The fluids pass only once
The heat is rejected to an external medium
checks.x: A regenerative heat exchanger is one in which the same fluid is both the cooling fluid and the cooled fluid.

checks.q: What does the term non-regenerative tell you about a heat exchanger?
o: How it functions in a system, not its construction or flow type
That it must be tube and shell
That it must be counter flow
That it has only one pass
checks.x: The term regenerative/nonregenerative only refers to how a heat exchanger functions in a system, and does not indicate any single type.

body.text: A radiator is an air-to-liquid heat exchanger. Hot coolant flows through the tubes, and cooler air over the outside of the tubes picks up the heat.
Air is a poor conductor of heat, so fins on the outside of the tubes maximize the heat transfer area.
Fins are common on most liquid-to-air heat exchangers and in some high efficiency liquid-to-liquid units.

In the condenser, hot, high pressure refrigerant gas condenses to a subcooled liquid. In the evaporator, cool refrigerant absorbs heat from air flowing over the tubes, which cools the air and boils the refrigerant.

checks.q: Which is a common application of a heat exchanger?
o: A strainer in a suction line
A pressure gauge on a tank
A radiator on an internal combustion engine
A check valve in a pump discharge
checks.x: Common applications include HVAC systems, radiators on internal combustion engines, boilers, condensers, and preheaters or coolers in fluid systems.

checks.q: Why do radiators have fins on their tubes?
o: Air is a poor conductor, so the heat transfer area must be maximized
To strengthen the tubes against pressure
To slow the coolant
To prevent corrosion
checks.x: Because air is such a poor conductor of heat, the heat transfer area is maximized by using fins on the outside of the tubes.

body.text: In a steam system, process steam is tapped off to heat the feedwater in preheater stages.

body.alt: U-tube feedwater heat exchanger: steam enters the shell from the top and condenses, while feedwater flows through the U-tubes.

body.text: The steam gives up sensible heat and latent heat of vaporization on the shell side. The shell side fluid level sets how many tubes are exposed to the hot steam, so it is very important to efficiency.

checks.q: Why is an input fluid preheated in stages?
o: It lowers the pressure of the fluid
It removes dissolved gases
It reduces the number of pumps
It increases plant efficiency and minimizes thermal shock stress
checks.x: Preheating in stages increases the plant's efficiency and minimizes thermal shock stress to components.

body.alt: Single-pass condenser: cooling water flows through straight tubes between water boxes while steam condenses on the shell side and collects in the hotwell.

body.text: A condenser turns used steam back into water for return as feedwater, and it raises cycle efficiency by letting the cycle operate with the largest possible delta-T and delta-P between source and heat sink.
Condensate collects in the hotwell, and the condensate pump takes its suction there.
A few degrees of subcooling prevents condensate pump cavitation. Excessive condensate depression lowers plant efficiency, because the subcooled condensate must be reheated.
An air ejector or vacuum pump establishes and helps maintain condenser vacuum, because air and other noncondensable gasses cannot be kept out.

checks.q: What is the purpose of a steam condenser?
o: To remove the latent heat of vaporization and condense the vapor into a liquid
To superheat the steam
To raise the turbine exhaust pressure
To remove sensible heat from feedwater only
checks.x: The purpose of a condenser is to remove the latent heat of vaporization, condensing the vapor into a liquid.

o: The top of the condenser, where steam enters
The water box at the tube inlet
The air ejector suction
The bottom area of the condenser, where condensate collects
checks.x: The bottom area of the condenser is the hotwell. This is where the condensate collects and the condensate pump takes its suction.

o: The drop in cooling water pressure
The level of water in the hotwell
How far the condensate is cooled below saturation temperature
The vacuum in the condenser
checks.x: Condensate depression is the difference between the saturation temperature for the existing condenser vacuum and the temperature of the condensate.

checks.q: Why are condensers in large steam cycles operated at a vacuum?
o: To prevent air from leaving the condenser
To increase the cooling water flow
To keep steam temperature and pressure as low as possible for highest cycle efficiency
To raise the boiling point of feedwater
checks.x: Condensers operate at a vacuum to ensure the temperature and pressure of the steam is as low as possible, which maximizes the delta-T and delta-P and the cycle efficiency.

body.text: Consider the difference in operating temperature between the two fluids when placing a heat exchanger in service, to prevent thermal shock.

checks.q: When securing a heat exchanger, which fluid is stopped first?
o: Whichever is at the higher pressure
The hot fluid
The cold fluid
Both at the same moment
checks.x: When securing a heat exchanger, first stop the hot fluid by shutting the discharge valve. Second, stop the colder fluid.

examples.title: Counter flow against parallel flow

fig.alt: Counter flow arrangement with its temperature graph.

examples.problem: The same heat exchanger runs first as counter flow and then as parallel flow. Hot fluid: 200°F in, 145°F out. Cold fluid: 80°F in, 120°F out. Uo = 70 BTU/hr-ft²-°F and Ao = 75 ft². Compare the heat transfer rates.
steps: ΔTlm = (ΔT2 - ΔT1) / ln(ΔT2 / ΔT1), and Q = Uo Ao ΔTlm.
Counter flow: the end differences are 200 - 120 = 80°F and 145 - 80 = 65°F, so ΔTlm = 15 / ln(80/65) = 72°F.
Parallel flow: the end differences are 200 - 80 = 120°F and 145 - 120 = 25°F, so ΔTlm = 95 / ln(120/25) = 61°F.
Counter flow: Q = 70 x 75 x 72 = 3.8 x 10^5 BTU/hr.
Parallel flow: Q = 70 x 75 x 61 = 3.2 x 10^5 BTU/hr.
examples.answer: Counter flow transfers more heat under the same conditions: 3.8 x 10^5 BTU/hr against 3.2 x 10^5 BTU/hr.

facts.q: What are the two types of heat exchanger construction?
What are the four internal parts of a tube and shell heat exchanger named in DOE-HDBK-1018?
facts.a: Tubes, tube sheet, shell, and baffles.

facts.q: What is cross flow in a heat exchanger?
facts.a: One fluid flows perpendicular to the second, at a 90° angle. It is usually used where one fluid changes state.
The bottom area of a condenser, where condensate collects and the condensate pump takes its suction.
The amount the condensate is cooled below saturation temperature, in degrees subcooled.

facts.q: Why do large steam condensers run at a vacuum?
facts.a: To keep steam temperature and pressure as low as possible, which maximizes the difference between source and heat sink for highest cycle efficiency.

summary.text: Most heat exchangers are tube and shell or plate. The main internal parts are the tubes, tube sheet, shell, and baffles.
Parallel flow runs in the same direction, counter flow in opposite directions, and cross flow at 90°. Counter flow is the most efficient.
Multi-pass units pass the fluids more than once. Regenerative units use the same fluid for heating and cooling.
Applications include preheaters, radiators, air conditioning evaporators and condensers, and steam condensers.
Admit the colder fluid first, stop the hot fluid first, and vent before placing the unit in service.
